title: How to Plan for Retirement When You Expect Future Caregiving Responsibilities
description: Budgeting for the financial support of a spouse or adult child.
content:
Retirement planning usually assumes you only need to support yourself. But what if you are the safety net for someone else? Whether it is a spouse with a degenerative condition, an adult child with special needs, or aging parents, 'Caregiving Risk' is a massive liability. It requires a larger portfolio, specialized legal structures (Trusts), and a conservative withdrawal strategy to ensure the money lasts for *two* lives, not just one.

Key Takeaways

  • The 'Two-Person' Budget: You cannot plan for expenses to drop. If you are caring for someone, expenses (medical, housing, therapy) often rise in retirement. Budget for 120% of current spending, not 80%.
  • Life Insurance in Retirement: Usually, you drop life insurance when you retire. If you have a dependent, you must keep it. You need a permanent death benefit (or long-term Term policy) to fund their care if you die first.
  • Special Needs Trusts: If supporting a disabled child/adult, never leave money directly to them. It disqualifies them from government benefits (SSI/Medicaid). Use a Special Needs Trust.
  • Preserve Liquidity: Caregiving requires cash. You cannot lock up all your money in an annuity. Keep a larger 'Cash Bucket' (2-3 years) to handle sudden medical equipment or care facility costs.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Medicaid is the payer of last resort. If you support a spouse, you must understand 'Spousal Impoverishment' rules—how to split assets so the healthy spouse isn't bankrupted by the sick spouse's nursing home bills.

The Caregiver's Portfolio

You need a 'Forever Fund'.

1. The 'Sinking Fund' for Care

Estimate the future cost.
Example: Memory Care facility in 10 years ($8k/mo).
Action: Invest specifically for this liability. Do not commingle it with your travel fund.

2. Social Security Optimization

Strategy: The healthy caregiver must delay claiming Social Security until 70.
Why: This maximizes the survivor benefit. If the caregiver dies, the dependent needs the maximum possible guaranteed income stream.

3. Asset Protection

If you are sued (e.g., car accident), your personal assets are at risk. A dependent relies on those assets.
Fix: Umbrella Insurance ($2M policy). It costs $300/year and shields the nest egg.

Legal & Logistics

  1. ABLE Accounts: For disabled dependents (onset before age 26), contribute to an ABLE account. It grows tax-free and can be used for housing/food without hurting SSI eligibility.
  2. Letter of Intent: Write a manual for the next caregiver. Doctors, medications, routines, financial accounts. If you have a stroke, who takes over?
  3. Guardian Nomination: Update your Will. Name a successor guardian for your dependent. Ensure that person is willing and funded.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I get paid to be a caregiver?

In some states, Medicaid waivers allow family members to be paid a small stipend for providing home care. Check your state's HCBS programs.

Should I buy LTC insurance for my spouse?

If they are already diagnosed, you can't. If they are healthy but high risk (family history), buy it in your 50s. Once you need it, it's too late.

What is a joint annuity?

It pays income as long as either person is alive. Always choose 'Joint and Survivor 100%' payout. It pays less per month, but ensures the dependent never sees a pay cut.
